title: Binyan Yehoshua on Avot D'Rabbi Natan
heTitle: בנין יהושע על אבות דרבי נתן
text: "Our ancestors" — Meaning our teachers, who are called "fathers," as it says (2 Kings 2:12), "Elisha called out to Elijah, 'My father, my father,'" because he was his teacher. And in the Moed Katan 26, it says: "Father — this refers to one’s teacher who taught him wisdom."
"If they had known" — This refers to their careful consideration of their words, meaning that the intent of their ancestors was to teach that they served [God] without expecting a reward.

"They would not have said" — Their mistaken belief concerned the resurrection of the body. Since they heard that people should serve God out of love and that their reward would be doubled in the World to Come, they surely believed in reward and punishment. However, their erroneous view was that while the soul would receive its reward in Gan Eden with great delight, the body would return to dust and have no reward. They denied only the resurrection of the body, not the concept of reward. This is why they scrutinized the language, saying, "Is there a labourer who works all day and does not receive his wages?" — alluding to the physical body that toils all day, only for its efforts to be in vain. Therefore, they concluded, "If our ancestors had known" — meaning they did not believe that the physical body would return as it was to receive eternal reward, since it is made of dust and returns to dust.

"And they would use" — This refers to Antigonus and his students, who were wealthy and would use silver and gold utensils. Nevertheless, their hearts were not arrogant because of this, as explained in the earlier teaching.

"That not" — And in some texts, it reads: "And their hearts were not arrogant about it." This is what Tzadok and Boethus would say: Even though the Pharisees use silver and gold vessels, they are not arrogant about it. Rather, it is a tradition in their hands, meaning a received teaching, and there is no reason for unnecessary suffering — that is, for the body, as mentioned above. See also Rashbam in Bava Batra 115b, who brings this teaching from Avot D'Rabbi Natan, and in Tosefot Yom Tov on Chapter 1, Mishnah 11.

withhold this is the language of deduction. As it comes in Pesachim 118a "The Holy Blessed One does not withhold reward from any creature". And in the whole Talmud [...]. And so the explanation is, withheld the creatures from the urge to evil and from evil deeds, and brought them under the wings of the Divine Presence.
You have bound yourself that in the world to come, that you begot a mamzer. That this is from sin that it is not possible to mend, as it comes in Chagiga 9b.

That a mamzer does not enter Jerusalem. Even though it says at the end of Tractate Horayot (Horayot 3:8) that a learned mamzer precedes an ignoramus high priest. As it says (Proverbs 3:15) "She [wisdom] is more precious than rubies", from a high priest who enters within and beyond. Nonetheless, the holiness of Jerusalem is unable to bear him, since its holiness is very great -- one who does not have proper lineage, such as a mamzer, would not be able to have settlement in Jerusalem. And so it is written "And a mamzer shall dwell in Ashdod, etc." (Zechariah 9:6). Commentated.

One who learns Torah in their youth does not forget easily, as stated earlier that they are like fresh parchment. It turns out that when something is difficult in one place, they resolve it by means of a different topic elsewhere, for words of Torah are poor in one place and rich in another. If so, this one has in their hand healing medicine. However, the old person who forgets doesn't have this healing, only the scalpel to cut, for the difficulty is in a "poor place".
